extras.title: Kenmu Restoration
extras.note: A brief attempt by Emperor Go-Daigo to restore direct imperial rule; the later Southern Court continued after the Ashikaga seized Kyoto.

extras.title: Azuchi–Momoyama · unification
extras.note: Selected political frame for Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Tokugawa consolidation. Art histories often extend the Momoyama period to 1615; it is not a single hereditary dynasty.

extras.title: Korean Empire
extras.note: Gojong proclaimed an empire in 1897 within the continuing Yi royal house. Japan imposed a protectorate in 1905 before annexation in 1910.

extras.title: Korea under Japanese rule
extras.note: Japanese colonial administration over Korea; Korean resistance, culture and independence movements continued. Colonial government did not represent voluntary political union.

extras.title: Northern Korea · Soviet occupation
extras.note: The northern occupation zone after Japanese surrender; local politics and competing projects developed within a Soviet military framework. This was not yet the DPRK at its creation in 1945.

extras.title: Southern Korea · U.S. military government
extras.wikiTitle: United States Army Military Government in Korea
extras.note: The southern occupation zone after Japanese surrender, preceding the Republic of Korea. Local political struggles and violence are not captured by a simple line of institutional succession.

extras.title: Dutch East India Company · island Southeast Asia
extras.note: Selected VOC activity in the Indonesian archipelago, not the company’s full Asian reach or uniform control of every island. Local states remained independent or negotiated and fought with the company.

extras.title: Dutch East Indies
extras.note: Colonial administration succeeded VOC rule in stages, with British interregnum and later Japanese occupation. Dutch territorial claims were resisted and did not imply uniform control from 1800.

extras.title: Japanese occupation · East Indies
extras.wikiTitle: Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies
extras.note: Japanese military occupation displaced Dutch colonial government during the Second World War; it was not Indonesian independence.

extras.title: Cambodian kingdoms after Angkor
extras.note: Cambodian courts and capitals continued after Angkor’s political decline amid changing relations with Siam and Vietnam; neither Khmer society nor Angkor’s religious significance ended in 1431.

extras.title: French protectorate of Cambodia
extras.note: French colonial control coexisted with a Cambodian monarchy; Japanese wartime intervention and the brief 1945 independence episode interrupted the wider protectorate frame.

extras.title: Cambodia · independent kingdom
extras.note: Independent monarchy and Sihanouk-led political order before the 1970 coup; Sihanouk abdicated the throne in 1955 but remained a dominant political leader.

extras.title: Khmer Republic
extras.note: Lon Nol’s republican regime emerged after Sihanouk’s removal amid widening regional warfare and civil war.

extras.title: Khmer Rouge · Democratic Kampuchea
extras.note: Khmer Rouge rule began with the capture of Phnom Penh in April 1975; the formal Democratic Kampuchea constitution followed in 1976. Forced labour, persecution, mass deaths and genocide marked this regime.

extras.title: People’s Republic / State of Cambodia
extras.note: Vietnamese-backed government controlled most of Cambodia while war and international recognition disputes continued; renamed State of Cambodia in 1989, before the 1991 settlement and 1992–1993 UN transition.

extras.title: Cambodia · restored kingdom
extras.note: Constitutional monarchy restored after the Paris peace process, UN-sponsored elections and 1993 constitution. Restoration of the royal institution did not erase the preceding republics, wars or their effects.

extras.title: Nguyễn dynasty
extras.note: The last Vietnamese royal dynasty continued at Huế after France imposed colonial rule. Its dynastic lifespan must not be equated with uninterrupted sovereignty over modern Vietnam.

extras.title: French Indochina
extras.note: A colonial federation developed through conquests and protectorates over different territories, including Vietnam, Cambodia and later Laos; Japanese wartime control and independence movements interrupted the frame.

extras.title: Democratic Republic of Vietnam
extras.note: Independence proclaimed in 1945; the government controlled the northern regroupment zone after the 1954 agreements and later won the war. This was not a state first founded in 1954.

extras.title: Southern Vietnam · State and Republic
extras.note: Selected umbrella for the State of Vietnam from 1949 and the Republic proclaimed in 1955; administrative control and borders were contested throughout the wars.

extras.title: Northern Yuan and post-Yuan Mongol courts
extras.note: After losing the main Chinese realm, Yuan rulers retreated to Mongolia; successor courts and confederations competed with Oirat powers. Later regional Mongol histories extended beyond the Northern Yuan dynastic endpoint.

extras.title: Khalkha Mongol principalities
extras.location: Mongolian plateau north of the Gobi
extras.note: Selected regional political frame north of the Gobi, not the full lifespan of Khalkha people. This branch is not identical to all Mongols or every Northern Yuan successor polity.

extras.title: Bogd Khanate of Mongolia
extras.note: Independence declared in 1911, with contested autonomy and Chinese military reoccupation in 1919; the Bogd Khan returned in 1921 before the 1924 republic.

extras.title: Mongolian People’s Republic
extras.note: A Soviet-aligned socialist state, not a Soviet Union constituent republic. The democratic revolution began in 1990 before the constitutional state-name change in 1992.

extras.title: Mongolia · democratic constitutional era
extras.note: The peaceful democratic transition began in 1990 and a new constitution followed in 1992; this was a change of political system within a continuing state, not the origin of Mongolian people.

maps.title: China · early cultures and dynasties

connections.label: Jade traditions endure
connections.summary: Liangzhu jade traditions influenced later Bronze Age centres, including late Shang Anyang.
connections.note: This cultural legacy crosses a substantial chronological gap; it is not a claim of direct dynastic succession or a Liangzhu–Xia state lineage.

connections.label: Traditional sequence
connections.summary: Later histories place Xia before Shang in a dynastic sequence.
connections.note: Xia remains unconfirmed in contemporary inscriptions; this dashed link records historiography, not a securely attested conquest or identification of Erlitou.

connections.label: Zhou conquest
connections.summary: Zhou forces overthrew the Shang ruling house.
connections.note: The conventional date does not imply that Shang populations and cultural practices disappeared.

connections.label: Qin consolidation
connections.summary: Qin ended the Zhou royal house and later conquered the other Warring States before proclaiming an empire.
connections.note: Zhou kingship ended in 256 BCE; imperial unification followed in 221 BCE, so the two plotted period boundaries do not mark a single instantaneous transfer.

connections.label: Rebellion and Han rule
connections.summary: After Qin collapse and civil war, Liu Bang established Han rule and took the imperial title in 202 BCE.
connections.note: Han dates conventionally begin with Liu Bang’s kingdom in 206 BCE; this is a change of regime, not uninterrupted Qin government.

connections.label: Han breaks apart
connections.summary: The end of Han rule gave way to competing kingdoms and subsequent northern and southern dynasties.
connections.note: The Age of Division is a period containing many governments, including a brief Western Jin reunification, rather than a successor state.

connections.label: Sui reunification
connections.summary: Sui replaced Northern Zhou in 581 and conquered the southern Chen in 589.
connections.note: Northern and southern political consolidation occurred in stages; the period and dynasty intentionally overlap.

connections.label: Tang takes power
connections.summary: Li Yuan established the Tang dynasty amid the collapse of Sui authority.
connections.note: Early Tang consolidation continued after the dynastic proclamation.

connections.label: Competing realms
connections.summary: Tang collapse left successive northern dynasties and concurrent southern kingdoms.
connections.note: This umbrella period does not represent one united government or just five rulers of all China.

connections.label: Song consolidation
connections.summary: The Song foundation in 960 was followed by campaigns against several remaining independent kingdoms.
connections.note: Other states including Liao continued outside Song rule; 960 did not reunify all territory in modern China.

maps.note: Archaeological influence, later tradition and political change are distinct links. Continue from Song in the existing Mongols and China map for Yuan, Ming, Qing, ROC, PRC and Taiwan-era histories.

maps.title: Japan · cultures, courts and shogunates

connections.label: Agriculture and migration
connections.summary: Wet-rice farming and continental exchanges transformed communities while some Jōmon practices continued.
connections.note: These are overlapping regional archaeological classifications, not two empires or the replacement of an entire people; the transition has no single nationwide date.

connections.label: Regional state formation
connections.summary: Growing regional powers and monumental tomb building accompanied the emergence of Yamato political dominance.
connections.note: This is a long social and political process; the Kofun-period boundary is not an exact founding date for Japan or one securely identified conquest.

connections.label: Court moves to Nara
connections.summary: The court moved its capital from the Asuka region to Nara.
connections.note: A change of capital and historical period within developing court institutions, not a new people replacing the Yamato population.

connections.label: Capital at Heian
connections.summary: The imperial capital moved to Heian-kyō, present-day Kyoto.
connections.note: The court first moved through the Nagaoka capital, 784–794; the label condenses that transition.

connections.label: Embassies and statecraft
connections.summary: Court missions and imported models connected Tang China with Japan’s Nara court.
connections.note: Japanese missions to Tang China began earlier, in 630; this edge selects exchanges during the Nara period (710–794). Diplomatic and cultural exchange did not make Japan a province of Tang China.

connections.label: Warrior government
connections.summary: Minamoto victory in 1185 established a military regime at Kamakura, with Yoritomo named shogun in 1192.
connections.note: The imperial court continued; this marks a shift in political power rather than the end of the imperial institution.

connections.label: Failed invasions · 1274 & 1281
connections.summary: Mongol-led Yuan expeditions attacked Japan but failed to establish control.
connections.note: This is a conflict link, not successful conquest. Goryeo and other forces participated; Japan was not incorporated into Yuan rule.

connections.label: Shogunate overthrown
connections.summary: Go-Daigo and his supporters overthrew the Kamakura shogunate.
connections.note: The imperial revival was brief, while conflict over rival courts continued after it ended.

connections.label: Ashikaga ascendancy
connections.summary: Ashikaga Takauji displaced Go-Daigo in Kyoto and subsequently became shogun.
connections.note: Northern and Southern courts competed until 1392; this is not a peaceful complete transfer of national control.

connections.label: Nobunaga takes Kyoto
connections.summary: Nobunaga entered Kyoto and later removed the last Ashikaga shogun.
connections.note: Regional wars and Toyotomi consolidation followed; the Sengoku conflicts overlap these named periods.

connections.label: Tokugawa government
connections.summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu’s ascendancy led to a shogunate based in Edo.
connections.note: The imperial court and regional domains continued, and Toyotomi resistance was not eliminated until 1615.

connections.label: Meiji Restoration
connections.summary: The Tokugawa shogunate fell and a new government claimed to restore imperial authority.
connections.note: Modern Japan includes later imperial, wartime, occupation and constitutional phases; 1868 is not Japan’s founding.

maps.note: Archaeological periods are not states, and courts and shogunates could coexist. Cross-map Japanese expansion and Korea appear in Korea’s map.

maps.title: Korea · dynasties, colonisation and division

connections.label: Mongol invasions
connections.summary: Mongol invasions devastated Goryeo before negotiated submission and later close dynastic ties.
connections.note: Goryeo retained its royal house; invasion and subordinate relations did not simply turn it into a replacement Chinese dynasty.

connections.label: Court and marriage ties
connections.summary: Goryeo and Yuan courts developed close political relations, including royal intermarriage.
connections.note: These unequal ties coexisted with Goryeo institutions; later Goryeo rulers contested Yuan influence.

connections.label: New royal dynasty
connections.summary: Yi Seonggye deposed the last Goryeo ruler and founded Joseon.
connections.note: A change of ruling house and political institutions within Korean history, not the origin of Korean people.

connections.label: Empire proclaimed
connections.summary: Gojong adopted the imperial title and renamed the state the Korean Empire.
connections.note: The timeline’s broad Joseon block extends to 1910 by dynastic convention; this node distinguishes the state-name change within that royal house.

connections.label: Japanese annexation
connections.summary: Japan annexed Korea after extending control through an imposed protectorate.
connections.note: Japan’s own government continued; the two source nodes identify the colonising state and the annexed Korean monarchy, not two equal partners in a union.

connections.label: Liberation and occupations
connections.summary: Japanese surrender ended colonial rule and Soviet and U.S. forces occupied zones divided at the 38th parallel.
connections.note: The military division was imposed amid liberation and did not immediately create the two states established in 1948.

connections.label: Republic established
connections.summary: The Republic of Korea was established in the southern zone.
connections.note: This followed a contested state-building process; the zone-to-state link does not imply unanimous consent or settled all-Korea sovereignty.

connections.label: DPRK established
connections.summary: The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea was established in the northern zone.
connections.note: Both new governments claimed to represent Korea; this map describes administration without adjudicating those competing claims.

connections.label: War and armistice
connections.summary: North Korean invasion opened a war involving both Korean states and international forces, ending in an armistice.
connections.note: A conflict link, not state succession; the armistice suspended fighting and did not itself provide a final peace settlement.

maps.note: This map follows the histories already in the atlas and does not claim to start Korean history with Goryeo. Division in 1945 and state establishment in 1948 are separate events.

maps.title: Maritime Southeast Asia · encounters and independence

connections.label: Buddhist journeys
connections.summary: The Tang-era monk Yijing studied and translated Buddhist texts at Srivijaya while travelling between China and India.
connections.note: A scholarly and maritime connection, not Chinese annexation or a single route followed by every traveller.

connections.label: Chola naval raid
connections.summary: Chola forces raided Srivijaya’s maritime realm.
connections.note: A raid and episode of warfare, not proof that Chola permanently replaced Srivijaya across its trading network.

connections.label: Mongol expedition repelled
connections.summary: A Yuan expedition into Java was defeated during the conflicts surrounding Majapahit’s foundation.
connections.note: The invaders did not establish lasting Yuan rule; the state’s foundation involved local struggles beyond this selected encounter.

connections.label: Literary legacy
connections.summary: Modern Indonesia adopted its national motto from the Majapahit-era poem Kakawin Sutasoma.
connections.note: A documented modern reception of a literary phrase, not direct political succession, unchanged borders or descent of all Indonesians from one empire.

connections.label: Company to colonial state
connections.summary: The Dutch government took over VOC possessions after the company’s dissolution.
connections.note: Expansion of colonial control continued over the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; many local states had independent histories beyond the VOC’s reach.

connections.label: Japanese occupation
connections.summary: Japanese conquest displaced Dutch colonial administration in the East Indies.
connections.note: This represents wartime military rule rather than a voluntary transfer or liberation into an independent state.

connections.label: Independence proclaimed
connections.summary: Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed Indonesian independence after Japan’s surrender.
connections.note: Dutch attempts to restore colonial control led to a further revolution and war; independence was not uncontested or fully recognised on proclamation day.

connections.label: Sovereignty transferred
connections.summary: Dutch recognition and transfer of sovereignty in 1949 were followed by a unitary Indonesian republic in 1950.
connections.note: Territorial integration remained incomplete, notably in western New Guinea; this is not a claim that all present borders were settled in 1949.

maps.note: Separate precolonial encounters and cultural reception are shown alongside the colonial-to-independent state sequence. There is no asserted Srivijaya→Majapahit→Indonesia governmental lineage.

maps.title: Cambodia and Vietnam · courts, colonies and modern states

connections.label: Courts move south
connections.summary: Cambodian royal centres shifted southward as Angkor’s imperial power contracted.
connections.note: 1431 is a conventional political marker; Angkor was not wholly abandoned and Khmer people and culture continued.

connections.label: French protectorate
connections.summary: France established a protectorate over the Cambodian kingdom.
connections.note: The monarchy continued under colonial restriction; this is not a disappearance or replacement of Cambodian society.

connections.label: Colonial federation
connections.summary: Cambodia’s protectorate was incorporated into the French Indochinese federation.
connections.note: The protectorate and federation overlapped as different administrative levels, rather than one ending when the other began.

connections.label: Independence restored
connections.summary: Cambodia regained independence from France under the monarchy.
connections.note: The colonial federation’s final collapse in 1954 is a separate regional milestone.

connections.label: Coup and republic
connections.summary: Sihanouk’s removal was followed by the proclamation of the Khmer Republic.
connections.note: This regime change unfolded within civil war and international intervention, not a consensual national union.

connections.label: Khmer Rouge victory
connections.summary: Khmer Rouge forces captured Phnom Penh and imposed a new revolutionary regime.
connections.note: The takeover began the mass coercion and killings of Khmer Rouge rule; Democratic Kampuchea’s formal state constitution followed in 1976.

connections.label: Regime overthrown
connections.summary: Vietnamese invasion and Cambodian allied forces overthrew the Khmer Rouge government in Phnom Penh.
connections.note: Khmer Rouge forces continued fighting, and diplomatic representation remained contested; January 1979 did not bring immediate peace.

connections.label: Peace process and monarchy
connections.summary: The Paris peace process and UN transition led to elections and restoration of a constitutional monarchy in 1993.
connections.note: This condenses the 1989 State of Cambodia renaming and the multi-party transitional settlement; conflict did not cease instantly.

connections.label: French colonial expansion
connections.summary: French conquest and protectorate arrangements subordinated Vietnamese territories before federation in Indochina.
connections.note: Nguyễn monarchs remained at Huế until 1945 under colonial constraint; this edge does not imply the dynasty ended in 1887.

connections.label: Republic proclaimed
connections.summary: The Democratic Republic of Vietnam declared independence after the collapse of wartime Japanese control.
connections.note: French efforts to restore colonial authority led to further war; the proclamation did not bring immediate agreed sovereignty.

connections.label: Regroupment zones
connections.summary: French defeat and the Geneva settlement left rival northern and southern administrations divided near the 17th parallel.
connections.note: These were provisional military regroupment zones, not an agreed permanent international frontier; DRV dated from 1945, State of Vietnam from 1949, and the southern Republic from 1955.

connections.label: Victory and reunification
connections.summary: Northern victory in 1975 was followed by formal reunification as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in July 1976.
connections.note: A separate provisional revolutionary government administered the South in 1975–1976; the 1976 state was not founded through a peaceful voluntary merger of the two wartime governments.

maps.note: Two connected regional strands, with colonial and modern regime changes distinguished from enduring Khmer and Vietnamese communities. Ancient Vietnamese dynasties not already in the timeline are outside this selected expansion.

maps.title: Mongolia · after the Yuan

connections.label: Yuan court retreats
connections.summary: Yuan rulers withdrew to Mongolia after losing their main Chinese realm.
connections.note: Ming replacement in China did not end the Yuan ruling line or Mongol political histories; this is a different branch from Ming succession.

connections.label: Regional Mongol powers
connections.summary: Post-Yuan Mongol politics developed into competing confederations and principalities, including the Khalkha north of the Gobi.
connections.note: Khalkha were one regional grouping among Oirat, Chahar and others; this is not a single clean division in 1635 or a claim that Khalkha alone inherited the Yuan.

connections.label: Khalkha submit to Qing
connections.summary: Khalkha princes entered Qing rule in 1691.
connections.note: Mongol groups entered Qing rule at different dates; 1691 applies to this Khalkha branch, not all Mongolia.

connections.label: Independence declared
connections.summary: Outer Mongolian leaders declared independence under the Bogd Khan as Qing authority collapsed.
connections.note: Recognition and autonomy remained contested, and Chinese forces reoccupied the territory in 1919.

connections.label: Chinese reoccupation
connections.summary: Chinese forces reimposed control before being expelled during the upheavals of 1921.
connections.note: This is a temporary occupation episode within the interrupted khanate frame, not permanent annexation or a direct line into today’s PRC.

connections.label: Republic proclaimed
connections.summary: After the 1921 revolution and the Bogd Khan’s death, a people’s republic was proclaimed.
connections.note: Soviet influence was strong, but Mongolia did not become one of the USSR’s constituent republics.

connections.label: Democratic transition
connections.summary: A peaceful democratic movement led to multi-party change and a new constitutional era.
connections.note: 1990 marks the political revolution and 1992 the new constitution; Mongolian state and social histories continued across that change.

maps.note: A selected Outer Mongolian branch from the Yuan, distinct from the Chinese dynastic sequence and from other Mongol successor states. Present-day Mongolia was never a Soviet constituent republic.

caveats: Existing mongols-china map already supplies Ming, Qing, ROC/PRC/Taiwan links; keep those relationships when merging this proposal.
The extra Mongolia map was requested by the modern-branches researcher to keep the Northern Yuan branch from disappearing into the Chinese dynastic succession.
Six maps are proposed, rather than five, because mainland and maritime Southeast Asia and the Northern Yuan branch each need their own coherent treatment.
Xia traditional sequence must remain dashed/contact with Tradition certainty; do not render as confirmed conquest.
Contact includes cultural transmission and modern reception as well as diplomatic/war encounters; it never asserts direct state descent.
Dates for archaeological periods, overlapping courts and colonial administrative layers require the qualifications provided; do not infer state extinction from any chart endpoint.
All 36 current East Asia histories are covered by new or existing map nodes; this does not claim comprehensive coverage of every East or Southeast Asian polity.
